column1: “Food at the market is too expensive. I can't feed my family.”
column2: You're right, and many families feel it. Food prices rose again this year, especially where transport costs went up. Some staples did get cheaper: garri and beans cost far less in early 2026 than a year before. But the job isn't done, and the next step is cheaper transport and safer farms.
column3: NBS: 1kg white garri ₦1,268 (Jan 2025) → ₦772 (Jan 2026); brown beans down ~49%. Food inflation was 19.59% in September 2026.

column1: “The government says inflation is falling, but prices keep rising.”
column2: Both are true. Falling inflation means prices are rising more slowly, not going back down. Headline inflation is down to about 15%, but food inflation has climbed again in 2026. So the pain you feel at the market is real.
column3: Headline 14.63% (Sept 2026). Food inflation rose from 8.89% (Jan 2026) to about 19.6% (Sept 2026). Never say the cost of living has fallen.

column1: “The minister said food prices crashed by 50%. That's a lie.”
column2: I won't defend that line; it went too far. What the official data shows is that some staples, like beans and garri, fell by 40–49% between January 2025 and January 2026. Others didn't, and many rose again later. It depends on the item and the market.
column3: NBS Selected Food Prices Watch (Jan 2026). The 50% claim was fact-checked by Dubawa. Don't repeat it.

column1: What are the main drivers of food prices in Nigeria?
column2: Transport and fuel costs (food travels from the North to Southern markets), insecurity on farms, the exchange rate for imported items, and levies along the roads. That's why falling inflation doesn't always reach the market quickly.
column3: Lagos markets saw 31 of 67 items rise in October 2026 even as national inflation fell.

column1: Why did food inflation drop so sharply in 2025 data?
column2: Partly real relief, partly technical: the NBS rebased the price index in 2025 to a newer base year, which lowered the year-on-year rate. Don't present the 2025 drop as all real price cuts.
column3: Food inflation fell to 13.12% in October 2025 from 39.16% a year earlier; NBS linked this partly to the rebasing.
